blocks.content: SQL ORDER BY covered controlling the order rows come back in. SQL LIMIT covers a closely related, genuinely practical concern, capping how many rows actually come back at all, rather than pulling back every single matching row when you only actually need a handful.

This topic covers why capping row count genuinely matters for real applications, why LIMIT should almost always be paired with ORDER BY, and how LIMIT combines with OFFSET to power page based results, a pattern that shows up constantly in real, user facing applications.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033209080-572746583.png
blocks.alt: SQL LIMIT covers capping how many rows actually come back, rather than pulling back every matching row when only a handful are needed

blocks.content: 1. Why Capping Row Count Genuinely Matters
blocks.text: 1. Why Capping Row Count Genuinely Matters

blocks.content: A real table can genuinely hold millions of rows, and most real use cases only actually need a small handful of them at once, the ten most recent orders, the top five highest paid employees, one specific page of search results.

Fetching every matching row when you only actually need a handful wastes real time processing the extra rows, and real network bandwidth transferring data your application will never actually use, both genuinely avoidable costs.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033210975-173465129.png
blocks.alt: A table can hold millions of rows, but most real use cases only need a handful, so fetching everything wastes real time and bandwidth

blocks.content: 2. LIMIT With Versus Without ORDER BY
blocks.text: 2. LIMIT With Versus Without ORDER BY

blocks.content: LIMIT with no ORDER BY genuinely means which specific rows actually come back is unpredictable, since without an explicit sort, the database is free to return whichever rows are internally convenient first, and that set can genuinely change between runs.

LIMIT paired with ORDER BY means the specific rows returned are genuinely predictable and repeatable, since you have explicitly defined which rows should logically be first, and LIMIT simply caps how many of that defined, ordered sequence actually come back.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033212547-794232900.png
blocks.alt: LIMIT without ORDER BY means which rows come back is genuinely unpredictable; LIMIT paired with ORDER BY makes the returned rows predictable and repeatable

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Using LIMIT alone with no ORDER BY, and expecting the same specific rows to come back consistently. Without an explicit sort, the database makes no promise about which rows you will actually receive within that limited set.
3. A Worked Example
A concrete query shows LIMIT paired correctly with ORDER BY to answer a genuinely common, real question.
SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;
blocks.code: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;

codes.sql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;

blocks.content: This query returns exactly the five highest paid employees, genuinely reliably, since the ORDER BY clause defines a clear, consistent ranking first, and LIMIT simply takes the top five rows from that already well defined, ordered sequence.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033214071-23268924.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: ORDER BY salary descending combined with LIMIT 5, returning exactly the five highest paid employees

blocks.content: 4. LIMIT Combined With OFFSET

OFFSET skips a given number of rows before LIMIT starts counting, which genuinely lets you fetch a specific slice of an ordered result, not just the very first rows. LIMIT then caps how many rows follow that skipped section.

Together, LIMIT and OFFSET genuinely power page based results, the pattern behind nearly every paginated list you have ever scrolled through in a real application, page two of search results, page three of a product catalog.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033215599-254193731.png
blocks.alt: OFFSET skips a given number of rows first, and LIMIT then caps how many rows follow, together powering page based results

5. A Worked Pagination Example
A concrete example shows this page based pattern in practice, fetching ten results per page from an ordered list, moving forward one page at a time.

Page one uses OFFSET 0 with LIMIT 10, fetching the first ten rows of the ordered result. Page two uses OFFSET 10 with LIMIT 10, skipping the first ten rows already shown, and returning the next ten. Page three continues that exact same pattern, OFFSET 20 with LIMIT 10, and so on for every subsequent page.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033217185-337818393.png
blocks.alt: A worked pagination example: page one uses OFFSET 0, page two uses OFFSET 10, page three uses OFFSET 20, each with LIMIT 10

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Large OFFSET values on a genuinely huge table can become slow, since the database often still has to scan past every skipped row internally, even though it does not return them. Deep pagination on very large tables is a genuinely real performance concern worth knowing about.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine LIMIT usage. Using LIMIT without ORDER BY and expecting stable, predictable results, missing the genuine unpredictability that comes from having no explicit sort defined. Using very large OFFSET values on a genuinely huge table, which can become surprisingly slow, since the database still has real work to do skipping past those rows internally.

And forgetting that LIMIT genuinely applies after ORDER BY, not before, meaning the sort always happens on the full matching result first, and LIMIT simply trims the already sorted result down afterward, a detail tied closely to SQL execution order, covered fully as its own topic shortly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784033218641-527974077.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: LIMIT without ORDER BY expecting stability, large OFFSET values becoming slow on huge tables, and forgetting LIMIT applies after ORDER BY

items: Using LIMIT with no ORDER BY at all: the specific rows returned are genuinely unpredictable without an explicit sort defined.
Relying on very large OFFSET values for deep pagination: can become genuinely slow on large tables, worth being aware of.
Assuming LIMIT filters before sorting happens: LIMIT genuinely applies to the already sorted result, after ORDER BY runs.
